newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Tanzania walks tight-rope on economic reforms.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania walks tight-rope on economic reforms.

text.p: Tanzania is walking an economic tight-rope, with only 20 percent of tax revenues available to run the government and develop infrastructure, Finance Minister Daniel Yona told Reuters.
Under a programme of donor-backed economic reform the government was spending only what it could raise in cash.

Of the average 45 billion Tanzanian shillings ($75 million) collected in taxes each month some 40 percent went on debt servicing and another 40 percent on salaries of state workers, Yona said in the Ethiopian capital of Addis Ababa where he was attending a financial conference.
"With a cash budget, we spend what we collect. There is no deficit. But for a government to run on only 20 percent and carry out development programmes, it is really a tight-rope.
"It is very hard on our people," Yona added. "It is hard for a government to tell its people there is simply no cash."

Yona said that the sale of public companies, originally listed at 400, was well on course with 150 so far sold. But he added that the big ones, such as telecommunications and power, were still to go and Tanzania was interested in offers.

"We want to speed up the process. The longer it takes the worst the institutions get," Yona said, adding that in the case of the telecommunications company, the government was still not sure what percentage it wanted sell.
He said so far 50,000 jobs had been slashed from a 350,000-strong civil service and donor support for retrenchment had helped the programme move along "very fast".

A lack of public awareness had delayed the establishment of the Dar es Salaam Stock Exchange although the regulatory Capital Markets Authority was in place and brokers and dealers had already been trained on market procedures, Yona said.

"It will be opened this year, exactly when I couldn't say. But it served no good purpose opening up the exchange with public awareness still too low. Now we have literature explaining the stock market being distributed," Yona said.
"The response is good. Public information is very important unless we want to flounder, which we must avoid."
He said 13 companies -- including the Tanzania Cigarette Co, Tanzania Breweries, General Tyres and Tanzania Oxygen -- would be the first to be listed whenever the exchange was opened.

Tanzania's economy was virtually ruined under the socialist policies of its first President Julius Nyerere, who lost power in 1985. Economic reforms have gathered pace under President Benjamin Mkapa, elected 15 months ago.

Yona said Tanzania was drawing from a three-year International Monetary Fund soft-loan facility worth $240 million. Some $40 million had already been disbursed and another $40 million was expected in six months provided Tanzania stayed on the path of reform, he said.
Tanzania was also in line for loans under the World Bank Structural Adjustment Credit (SAC), probably in May or June, Yona said. But he gave no specific figures.
Yona was in Addis Ababa to attend a meeting of African finance ministers focusing on debt and financial reforms.

"There is no hope for us if this debt burden cannot be tackled and tackled quickly. It is a huge burden," Yona said. He did not give specific figures for total debt or servicing costs. ($1=598 Tanzanian shillings).
